extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, mathematical educators, and the mathematical community
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how mathematicians should produce, present, validate, and value mathematical work — emphasizing human understanding, communication, social validation, and the varied roles of proofs and infrastructure in mathematical progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goal: advance human understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: What mathematicians accomplish is to advance human understanding of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics, not merely by counting theorems proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs should provide human understanding as well as correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs ought to give human understanding in addition to establishing that a theorem is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversy over computer-assisted proofs (e.g., Appel–Haken) reflects a desire for humanly comprehensible arguments; aim for explanations that convey why the result is true, not just that it is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate ways of thinking, not just definitions/theorems/proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical communication must convey the 'ways of thinking' and mental models behind results, not only formal statements and derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers, talks, and notes should include intuition, motivation, and the mental infrastructure so that outsiders can build the same understanding; avoid translating all insight into sterile formalism that loses the original human flavor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple modes of conception for concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Present mathematical concepts in several complementary ways (infinitesimal, symbolic, logical, geometric, rate, approximation, microscopic, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People understand differently; offering several conceptions helps a broader audience internalize the idea and connect with their own mental faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor exposition to the audience's mental infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs and explanations depend on the audience: what is two minutes for one group may take an hour for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the audience (subfield, analysts vs topologists, students vs experts) and provide the appropriate amount of background, examples, and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document background and infrastructure to lower entry barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Write and publish background, definitions, and explanatory material so others can learn the subject; avoid leaving essential infrastructure only in your head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to document infrastructure (as in the foliations example) raises entry barriers and can lead to the field's decline; distribute notes, give accessible lectures, and expand explanations in papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and credit a broad range of mathematical activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and reward activities beyond proving theorems: building infrastructure, explaining ideas, teaching, mentoring, computational experiments, and community-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The community’s overemphasis on theorem-credits is counterproductive; broader valuation will increase productivity and health of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proofs as clear and simple as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful proofs that will stand up to scrutiny are important; proofs should be written to make any weaknesses easy to detect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not weaken standards of proof, but emphasize clarity and simplicity so that errors are visible and fixable; supply details where needed and avoid unnecessary formal complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on social processes of validation while striving for rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical validity is often established by social standards and expert judgment as much as formal written verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts can accept high-level ideas before full details are checked (e.g., Wiles's proof); nevertheless, continue to supply details and participate in communal scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use names and unifying definitions to facilitate insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventing good names and unifying definitions (e.g., 'group', 'manifold') gives people handles for insights and aids communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, replace cumbersome circumlocutions with concise concepts that capture key structure and make ideas easier to teach and use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit multiple mental faculties in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Take advantage of language, visual/spatial intuition, logic, metaphor, stimulus-response procedures, and processes/time in explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include figures, physical metaphors, process descriptions, and mnemonic language to reach different ways people think; recognizing scale and spatial framing helps comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and explain the role a proof plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all proofs have the same role—some have lasting logical value, others have motivational or heuristic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether a proof is intended as a durable logical foundation, an illustration of a new way of thinking, or a temporary bridge; this affects how it should be documented and taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in social dissemination of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively use seminars, workshops, notes, and personal contact to spread understanding; the print medium alone is often inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-on-one communication and seminars use gestures, diagrams, and two-way Q&A that are crucial for transmitting subtle mental models; organize and participate in such exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about formalization efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalizing mathematics by computer is valuable and will teach us much, but it is costly and qualitatively different from current practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support formalization projects while recognizing practical limits: full formal correctness at scale would require massive rewriting and choices about definitions; aim to integrate interactive formal tools into mathematicians’ workflow where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate computer-verifiable formal correctness with human insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal proofs (computer-generated or checked) and human-understandable proofs serve different purposes; both are important but distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal completeness is often out of reach and presently mostly irrelevant to everyday mathematical practice; continue to value human-checkable explanations even as formal tools improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design teaching and assessment to test understanding, not rote skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework and tests should assess real understanding rather than reward superficial problem patterns or lenient grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid compensating for poor communication by lowering assessment standards; instead improve exposition and set assessments that require conceptual grasp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of foundational limitations and their practical impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations (set theory, well-orderings, Gödel incompleteness) are 'shakier' than everyday mathematics; treat foundational assumptions as pragmatic choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that some foundational principles are 'polite fictions' and that multiple consistent mathematical universes can exist; focus on practical utility rather than metaphysical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate the expansion factor when translating thought to paper
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often a big expansion from an idea in the author's head to a paper or talk; authors should work to reduce that gap for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide intermediate steps, motivations, and background so others do not need to reconstruct the missing mental infrastructure; include examples and explanations that mirror how the author actually thinks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridge subfield languages and cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage and support mathematicians conversant in multiple subfields to act as bridges, while being mindful of possible intimidation effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create environments, expositions, and mentorship that help cross-pollination without creating gatekeepers; reward work that helps others learn foreign subfield idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computations and experiments as insight-generating tools, not final proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational evidence and large computations can support conjectures and intuition but do not replace humanly understandable reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using computational approaches, strive to extract and communicate the underlying ideas and heuristics that explain the results to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make references and citations informative about assumed knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting results or techniques without proof, indicate what background is being assumed and provide references or people to consult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume readers will reconstruct missing sources; point to accessible sources or give enough detail for verification, since many 'generally known' facts lack a clear written origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct expositions that allow detection of flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Write arguments and proofs so that potential weaknesses or gaps can be readily detected by readers and colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break proofs into intermediate lemmas, state hypotheses clearly, and make dependencies explicit so the community can check and correct as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize team and network effects in producing results
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical progress is often a social/team effort; crediting only the final theorem-prover underestimates the contributions of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the roles of those who create the context, infrastructure, and supporting ideas; consider the team function (analogy: soccer players whose work enables the scorer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance publishing results with building community and mentoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about publishing, mentoring, and community-building affect the growth and longevity of a field and individuals' careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing less-than-perfectly-packaged theorems or withholding infrastructure can harm a field; invest time in mentoring, writing expository material, and promoting others' careers, even when this reduces personal theorem-credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the ephemeral or durable value of particular proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs may be superseded or become obsolete as the subject develops; others provide enduring conceptual frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether a proof is intended as a long-term logical cornerstone or as a means to introduce a new perspective; preserve material accordingly (exposition vs formal archiving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use seminars and interactive formats to convey difficult ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal and interactive venues (seminars, workshops, personal correspondence) are often the most effective at transmitting deep insights quickly within a subfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize and participate in such venues, and make accompanying written notes available to extend the reach of interactive explanations.
